title: Adversarial Déjà Vu: Jailbreak Dictionary Learning for Stronger Generalization to Unseen Attacks
one_liner: Jailbreak attacks unseen during training are not new tricks but remixes of old ones, so training on diverse combinations of attack skills beats training on isolated attacks.
lead: Large language models can be tricked into saying harmful things if you ask in the right (wrong) way—we call this a jailbreak. The old way to defend was to gather jailbreak examples and train the model to resist them. But new jailbreaks that were never seen during training still slip through. This paper's insight: jailbreaks unseen during training are not truly new. They are recombinations of attack techniques from papers published years earlier. By extracting those core techniques—call them adversarial skills—and training on different combinations of them, a model learns to resist attacks it has never encountered.

problem.h2: Why the old method fails on new attacks
paras: A jailbreak is a prompt that tricks a language model into producing harmful content by going around the safety training. Researchers publish new jailbreaks in papers every few months.

The natural defense is adversarial training: show the model examples of jailbreaks and train it to refuse them, just like showing a spam filter examples of spam. But here is the trap: when a brand new jailbreak appears (one the model never saw in training), the model is often still vulnerable. The training did not prepare it. This is the core problem.

Why does adversarial training fail? Because it teaches the model to block specific attacks, not to understand the attack strategy itself. It is like teaching a student the answer to every math problem in last year's test but not teaching them the underlying math—they will fail when the problems change.

callout.html: This paper extracts the core attack techniques from past jailbreaks, builds a library of them, trains on different combinations, and finds that models trained this way resist unseen attacks much better, because training on combinations teaches the model to recognize and block the underlying attack techniques, not just memorize surface patterns of specific attacks.

steps.text: Analyze 32 attack papers; find the core techniques (e.g. indirect requests, roleplay, encoding tricks).
Compress those skills into a small set of primitives; generate plain-English descriptions of each.
Show that unseen jailbreaks can be written as combinations of old skills—coverage grows, explanatory power grows.
Instead of training on single isolated attacks, train on diverse mixes of skill primitives.
Test on unseen jailbreaks; measure both success (blocks new attacks) and safety (does not refuse harmless queries).

paras: The paper shifts what the model trains on: instead of isolated jailbreak examples, it trains on diverse combinations of extracted adversarial skills.
object.object: training data: from single attacks to skill combinations

hidden.name: adversarial skill coverage
paras: Adversarial skill coverage is the fraction of a new jailbreak's core techniques that the model has already learned. For example, if Attack-E is made of 60% Skill-A and 40% Skill-C, and the model trained on both Skill-A and Skill-C combinations, then coverage is 100%. If the model only trained on Skill-A, coverage is 60%.

The paper measures this by extracting the adversarial skills from attack papers using an automated pipeline, building a dictionary, then asking: how much of an unseen attack can be explained as a combination of known skills? As skill coverage grows (more diverse combinations in training), the ability to predict and block unseen attacks grows monotonically—meaning it never dips, it only gets better—because the model has learned resistances to more of the underlying building blocks, so when a new attack mixes those blocks, the model can stop it.

heat.caption: Darker means more coverage of that attack by skills the model has trained on; highlights show which combos transfer to unseen attacks.

reads.html: Adversarial skill coverage is how much of a new jailbreak's recipe the model already knows. Train on more skill recipes, resist more new attacks.

The paper shows that unseen attacks have high explanatory power (coverage) via sparse composition of extracted skill primitives, and that expanding coverage is the key lever, not just scaling data size.

paras: The mechanism has three parts. First, adversarial skills are more general than specific attacks—a skill like 'indirect request' or 'roleplay' shows up in many different jailbreak papers. Training on many combinations of skills forces the model to learn what makes each skill dangerous, not just to memorize which attacks trigger refusals.

Second, jailbreaks unseen during training (Attack-E) are typically combinations of older skills (A + C). If the model has trained on different combinations of A and C, it has already learned to resist when A or C appear. It can recognize them in a new mixture, even if the exact mixture is new. This is why skill coverage—the fraction of the new attack's recipe the model knows—predicts whether the attack will succeed.

Third, training on combinations instead of isolated attacks prevents the model from finding narrow, attack-specific defenses that do not generalize. When you train only on Attack-A, the model might learn a shallow shortcut specific to how Attack-A is phrased. When you train on A+B, A+C, and A+D, the model must learn what A really is, at a deeper level, to handle it in context.

stages.s: Learned resistances to those skills activate
Model refuses or filters harmful output

math.words: The model minimizes the refusal loss across all skill combinations, weighted so that combinations with higher skill coverage are learned more strongly than combinations with low coverage.
symbols: fraction of the skill combo's primitives present in training examples
how often the model fails to refuse this particular skill combination
what the training algorithm minimizes; lower means better refusals

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Training data has: Skill-A alone (coverage 1.0), Skill-C alone (coverage 1.0), A+C (coverage 1.0).
New jailbreak Attack-F = A + Unknown skill (coverage 0.5, only A is known).
The model learned refusals for coverage 1.0 combos strongly. Attack-E (coverage 1.0) is resisted.
Attack-F (coverage 0.5) is only partially defended—the model has learned to resist A but not the unknown part.

math.note: Higher coverage of known skills means stronger learned resistances; the model refuses harder when it recognizes the attack recipe, because it has already trained on that skill in multiple contexts and knows how to block it.

bars.h2: How resistance to attacks improves with skill coverage

charts.title: Old method: train on isolated attacks
charts.note: Model memorized specific attacks but fails on new ones.

charts.title: ASCoT: train on skill combinations
charts.note: By training on skill combos, the model learns underlying patterns and resists attacks it has never seen.

items.html: If the extracted skill dictionary misses common attack primitives, new jailbreaks using those unseen skills will have low coverage and still succeed. The pipeline for extracting skills must be thorough.

Training on many combinations can cause the model to refuse harmless queries that coincidentally share words or structure with attack skills. The paper measures this and shows ASCoT keeps over-refusal low, but it remains a real tension.
An attacker who sees your skill dictionary could deliberately invent attacks that avoid all known skills (zero coverage). This is an arms race, not a solved problem.

Maintain a live, updated skill dictionary as new attacks appear. Train on broad, realistic combinations. Measure coverage of new attacks before deployment. Treat this as an ongoing process, not a one-time fix.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small jailbreak dataset of 5 known attacks. Extract their core skills (e.g. using an LLM to describe each attack's trick). Build combinations: A+B, A+C, B+C. Train a small language model on refusals to these combinations. Test on a held-out jailbreak (e.g. A+D) that uses known skills but is unseen. Measure: does the model refuse? Compare to a baseline trained only on single attacks. The demo should show that combination training generalizes better, because the model trained on A, B, C separately only learns shallow surface-pattern refusals, while the model trained on A+B, A+C, B+C must learn what each skill is at a deeper level to handle it in context.
demo.closing: The demo must show that a model trained on 10 skill combinations blocks more unseen attacks than a model trained on 10 isolated examples—because combinations teach the underlying skills, not surface patterns.
